title: Cortical dynamics during psychedelic and anesthetized states induced by ketamine
post: Aim: To characterise how the spatiotemporal complexity of EEG activity changes across subanesthetic and anaesthetic doses of ketamine. Methods: High-density scalp EEG in healthy volunteers during subanesthetic and anaesthetic ketamine. Hidden Markov modelling classified brain states, and Lempel-Ziv complexity was computed per state after controlling for spectral changes. Results: Subanesthetic ketamine raised complexity relative to baseline. Anaesthetic ketamine produced alternating low and high complexity before stabilising at a high level comparable to baseline. Conclusion: Ketamine-induced state transitions share features of anaesthesia, normal consciousness and altered consciousness, illustrating its complex pharmacological properties.

title: A Single Dose of Psilocybin Increases Synaptic Density and Decreases 5-HT2A Receptor Density in the Pig Brain
post: Aim: To test whether a single psilocybin dose changes synaptic density (SV2A) and 5-HT2A receptor density in the pig brain. Methods: Twenty-four awake pigs received psilocybin 0.08 mg/kg or saline intravenously and were euthanised at one or seven days. Autoradiography of hippocampus and prefrontal cortex used [3H]UCB-J, [3H]MDL100907 and [3H]Cimbi-36. Results: One day after psilocybin, hippocampal SV2A density was 4.42% higher and 5-HT2A density was lower in hippocampus and prefrontal cortex (−15.21% to −50.19%), significant for hippocampus across ligands and for prefrontal cortex with Cimbi-36 only. At seven days SV2A remained higher (+9.24% hippocampus, +6.10% prefrontal cortex), with no 5-HT2A differences. Conclusion: Psilocybin may cause persistent synaptogenesis and an acute fall in 5-HT2A density, possibly contributing to antidepressant effects.

title: Generational gains in cognitive capacity and dementia incidence rates in Western countries.
post: Aim: To test whether later-born generations enter old age with better memory and decline more slowly, and whether this explains falling dementia incidence. Methods: Analysis of about 783,000 episodic-memory assessments from about 219,000 individuals in five longitudinal studies followed up to 30 years, including hippocampal volumes. Results: Later-born generations showed higher memory levels in old age and slower subsequent decline, a double advantage large enough to plausibly account for the reported 13% per-decade fall in dementia incidence. Slower decline was mirrored by lower clinical impairment and slower hippocampal atrophy. Conclusion: Sustaining the dementia decline requires prevention that protects brain health across the lifespan, starting in childhood.
why_you: Relevant to your interest in brain health across the lifespan and computational psychiatry, though not a direct match to your current work.

title: The fate of poised pre-mRNAs shapes mitochondrial activity and cellular differentiation.
post: Aim: To determine how nuclear RNA quality control decides the fate of poised intron-containing polyadenylated pre-mRNAs. Methods: Molecular and genetic study in mouse and human cells, including NCBP3 depletion and pathogenic RNA exosome mutations, with analysis of mitochondrial function and motor behaviour. Results: NCBP3 favours splicing of poised pre-mRNAs while anillin favours exosome degradation; many affected transcripts encode mitochondrial factors. NCBP3 loss or exosome mutations reduced mitochondrial activity, causing muscle weakness, cerebellar hypomyelination and poorer motor coordination. Conclusion: A competition between pre-mRNA pathways controls mitochondrial function, and its disruption contributes to neurological disease.

title: Injury-induced signalling coordinates immunity and cannibalism in locusts.
post: Aim: To identify the molecular signal that draws cannibalistic locusts to injured conspecifics. Methods: Behavioural assays, olfactory receptor knockdowns, and bacterial gene-cluster deletions in Locusta migratoria, examining the symbiont-derived volatile guaiacol. Results: Guaiacol, released more after injury, attracts nymphs and triggers cannibalism via receptors LmOR36 and LmOR34. It is made by the symbiont Enterobacter hormaechei; deleting its gene cluster abolished production and behavioural effects. At low levels it activates immune pathways. Conclusion: A microbial-chemical signal links immune defence with cannibalism, offering molecular targets for population manipulation.

title: NeuroSim: a clinically informed multi-disorder EEG simulator with personalized pattern injection and AI-driven neurological modeling
post: Background: Deep learning for electroencephalography (EEG) based neurodiagnostics is constrained by the limited availability of labeled clinical recordings. Methods: Existing EEG simulators typically address a single disorder or trade biological interpretability for statistical fidelity. Results: A convolutional-attention classifier trained on simulated data reached 95.3 to 96.8 percent hold-out accuracy, and post hoc explainability analyses produced class-separable embeddings with attributions concentrated on pathophysiologically expected electrodes. Conclusion: NeuroSim is released as open-source software to support augmentation, benchmarking, and explainable artificial intelligence in neurological diagnostics.

title: Revisiting entropy and entropy-related magnitudes of a symbolic sequence and their estimation.
post: Aim: To revisit entropy, entropy density, effective measure complexity and informational distance, and how to estimate them for sequential data. Methods: Theoretical review linking Shannon entropy and Kolmogorov complexity, with estimation via Lempel-Ziv factorisation and an open-source parallel software library; three case studies on fMRI, coupled oscillators and ECG. Results: Ziv's theorem gives asymptotic equivalence between normalised distinct-word counts and entropy density, supporting estimation of these measures for finite sequences. Case studies illustrate applications to brain connectivity, oscillator dynamics and atrial fibrillation classification. Conclusion: The framework captures structural and dynamical properties across domains, with practical estimation tools for finite data.

title: The Association between Physical Activity and Higher Corticolimbic Synaptic Density is Independent of Body Mass Index.
venue: Biological psychiatry. Cognitive neuroscience and neuroimaging
venue_clean: Biological psychiatry. Cognitive neuroscience and neuroimaging
post: Aim: Whether physical activity is associated with higher synaptic density in corticolimbic regions of the living human brain. Methods: PET with [18F]SynVesT-1 in 51 individuals (61% female), grouped as physically active or insufficiently active; group comparisons, regression and mediation analyses including BMI and depressive symptoms. Results: Physically active participants had higher synaptic density across corticolimbic regions (F6,44 = 2.41, p = 0.042), remaining marginal after adjusting for BMI and depressive symptoms (p = 0.050). Region-specific associations were positive, and BMI did not mediate the relationships. Conclusion: Physical activity is associated with higher synaptic density, particularly in prefrontal circuits, partly independent of BMI. Longitudinal studies are needed to establish causality.

title: From antidepressants to psychedelics: revisiting the pharmacology of so-called serotoninergic treatments
post: Aim: Revisit the molecular mechanisms of antidepressants and OCD drugs to question whether SERT inhibition alone explains SSRI effects and psychedelic action. Methods: Narrative pharmacological review of the pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic properties of SSRIs and serotoninergic psychedelics, with focus on TrkB as a putative secondary target. Results: SSRI dosing needed for depression and OCD is consistent with a major target of much lower SSRI affinity than SERT, such as TrkB, which may offer a unifying account of antidepressant effects. Conclusion: TrkB may provide a unifying framework for antidepressant action, with implications for the therapeutic potential of psychedelics.

title: The diastole-systole transition as a regulatory window for heart-brain coupling in major depressive disorder: Evidence from cardiac phase-dependent 1/f slope and periodic neural dynamics.
post: Aim: Whether cardiac phase modulates periodic and aperiodic MEG activity differently in major depressive disorder. Methods: Simultaneous resting MEG and ECG in 60 patients and 60 matched controls, with a 6-month follow-up; SPRiNT separation of periodic and aperiodic activity; linear mixed models and permutation statistics. Results: Patients showed attenuated diastole-to-systole steepening of the left insular 1/f slope and greater late-systole delta reduction in the left anterior cingulate. Earlier posterior cingulate alpha peaks were also seen. Longitudinal insular changes in remitters were exploratory. Conclusion: Depression disrupts cardiac-cycle-dependent neural dynamics, with altered insular aperiodic modulation possibly reflecting excitation-inhibition and heart-brain synchrony changes.

title: Connectome modulates critical brain dynamics across local and global scales
post: Aim: How local near-criticality within brain regions interacts with global criticality when regions are coupled through a mouse connectome. Methods: Multiscale model with neural mass models tuned near the asynchronous-synchronous transition, coupled via an empirical mouse connectome, plus whole-brain simulations of connectome-coupled spiking neurons. Results: Local criticality was modulated by long-range coupling, producing nonlinear timescale gradients. Global criticality, with scale-free avalanches and optimal functional connectivity, emerged only when local populations were near criticality and coupled within an optimal range. Conclusion: Local and global criticality are dynamically intertwined but not directly aligned, and their relationship depends on structural connectivity.

title: Spectral and complexity-based signatures of advanced concentration absorption meditation: A high-density EEG study of jhana
post: Background: Advanced meditation provides structured and reproducible alterations of consciousness that are increasingly used as model states for the neuroscience of consciousness. Methods: We applied high-density EEG and a comprehensive multidimensional battery of spectral and complexity measures to characterize each ACAM-J state individually in 20 advanced meditators, together with phenomenological ratings. Results: ACAM-J produced widespread posterior-central reductions in oscillatory and aperiodic power, posterior aperiodic flattening across all eight states, and convergent increases in entropy-based complexity over the posterior cortex, with power effects strengthening with phenomenological depth. Conclusion: ACAM-J thus emerges as a non-pharmacological model state at the high-complexity end of the spectrum of altered consciousness, and reveals a previously unquantified dissociation between neural complexity and experiential richness for specific ACAM-J states.

title: Bridging Treatment Gaps in Adolescent Depression With Neuromodulation Targeting Anhedonia
post: Aim: Whether individualised functional connectivity-guided iTBS targeting left DLPFC improves depression and anhedonia in adolescents who have not responded to antidepressants. title: The Potency Stability Tradeoff: Evaluating EEG Biomarkers for Major Depressive Disorder.
post: Aim: Whether EEG biomarkers for major depressive disorder that are stable across data subsets generalise better than those with the strongest predictive signal. Methods: EEG from 30 MDD patients and 88 controls; connectivity, spectral and complexity features; XGBoost pipeline with leakage-free cross-validation and a nested Stability-Optimized Consensus Learning framework. Results: Theta and alpha features gave the strongest signal (max AUC 0.683) but were unstable across subsets (mean Jaccard 0.187) and overfitted. A model built on stable consensus biomarkers generalised better (AUC 0.792 vs 0.662) with less overfitting (P < .05). Conclusion: The MDD signature exists as a potent but unstable theta-alpha signal and a weaker but stable connectome signal. The authors argue stability matters more than strength for clinical biomarkers.

title: Bergenin ameliorates anxiety- and depression-like behavior in antibiotic-treated mice: behavioral and in silico insights.
post: Aim: Whether bergenin, an anti-inflammatory isocoumarin, reverses anxiety- and depression-like behaviour induced by antibiotic-driven gut dysbiosis in mice. Methods: Antibiotic regimen in Swiss albino mice followed by 14 days of bergenin (25 or 50 mg/kg/day) or fluoxetine; elevated plus maze, open field, forced swim and tail suspension tests; docking and 100 ns molecular dynamics against TLR4-MD-2 and SERT. Results: Bergenin dose-dependently attenuated anxiety- and depression-like deficits, with high-dose recovery of about 70-92%, without altering behaviour in antibiotic-free animals. In silico, it bound the SERT S1 site with stability resembling fluoxetine, but its TLR4-MD-2 interaction was shallow. Conclusion: Bergenin ameliorates behavioural deficits in antibiotic-treated mice, and in silico data favour serotonergic over TLR4 involvement. The authors stress that the work is hypothesis-generating and that microbiome and mechanistic assays were not performed.

title: Connectome Harmonic Analysis at 7 Tesla Reveals Selective Reorganization of Large-Scale Cortical Dynamics in Adult Users of Cannabis.
post: Aim: Whether cannabis use alters large-scale brain organisation, tested as changes in low-frequency connectome harmonics using 7T resting-state fMRI. Methods: Human Connectome Project 7T data from 81 cannabis users and 81 matched non-users; BOLD activity projected onto the first 200 connectome harmonics; t-tests with FDR correction and atlas localisation. Results: Cannabis users showed significantly greater power in one low-frequency harmonic (k = 6; t ≈ 4.19; p_FDR = 7.21 × 10⁻³; d = 0.659), roughly 44% higher than non-users, localised to a frontoparietal–sensorimotor network. It did not correlate with cannabis exposure variables, and behavioural associations did not survive FDR correction. Conclusion: Cannabis use is associated with selective amplification of one frontoparietal–sensorimotor eigenmode. The authors note the behavioural findings are nominal only.

title: Mechanism-aligned ketamine therapy for treatment-resistant depression: a 2026 update—toward an integrative mechanistic framework for clinical translation
post: Aim: Propose an integrative mechanistic framework for ketamine therapy in treatment-resistant depression, updating a 2021 systems-level model with literature through April 2026. Methods: Narrative review integrating evidence on NMDAR modulation, neuroplastogenesis, anti-inflammatory signalling, entropic brain states and psychedelic phenomenology, with attention to chronic stress and attachment as cross-cutting factors. Results: The review synthesises five interacting domains proposed to underlie rapid ketamine effects and considers how developmental and relational factors may shape treatment resistance across depression, PTSD and suicidality. Conclusion: The framework aims to generate testable predictions about patient selection, timing and durability of ketamine response, pending controlled evaluation.

title: Physics-informed neural networks for subject-specific recovery of travelling-wave structure in resting-state fMRI
post: Aim: Recover subject-specific travelling-wave structure from resting-state fMRI using a physics-informed neural network with a structural connectivity prior. Methods: A wave-informed physics-informed neural network modelling BOLD as seven damped travelling-wave generators anchored to Schaefer networks, validated on synthetic data and applied to 41 cognitively normal ADNI-3 participants with a diffusion-tensor prior. Results: The structural prior modestly but significantly increased alignment between recovered wave directions and white-matter geometry (one-sided Wilcoxon p = 0.026), with exploratory effects in visual, dorsal-attention and salience networks. Conclusion: The network-anchored parametric method returns subject-specific propagation descriptors from short scans, with the structural prior giving a small detectable benefit.

title: Sample size critically shapes the reliability of EEG case-control findings in psychiatry.
post: Aim: Quantify how sample size affects the reliability of EEG case-control findings across psychiatric conditions in children and adolescents. Methods: Resting-state EEG from 2,874 participants aged 5–18 years, including ADHD, autism, anxiety, learning disorders and controls, with spectral, temporal and complexity features compared across repeated random subsamples of varying size. Results: Small samples gave unstable, inflated and highly variable effect sizes, while larger samples converged on consistent but small effects. Statistical power rose steeply with sample size, while false positive rates stayed relatively stable. Conclusion: Sample size critically shapes EEG case-control outcomes, and conventional case-control designs may be limited for biomarker discovery in psychiatry.

title: Feasibility of Simulated Low-Count [18F]FDG PET/MR for Patients with Pediatric Epilepsy.
post: Methods: Twenty-seven pediatric patients with epilepsy were enrolled. List-mode PET data acquired over 20 min were truncated to 10, 7, and 4 min to simulate count reductions of 50%, 65%, and 80%, respectively. Results: Quantitative analysis showed that the contrast-to-noise ratio decreased and the coefficient of variation increased significantly with simulated count reduction. Both ROI-based and voxel-based methods demonstrated that EZ lateralization agreement with the clinical consensus did not decline with simulated count reduction. Conclusion: Our study in pediatric epilepsy suggests that a 65% simulated count reduction preserved clinically acceptable [ 18 F]FDG PET image quality, stable SUVR quantification, and concordance of EZ lateralization with the clinical consensus.

title: Reconsidering the Psychotomimetic Properties of LSD: Connectome-Based Classification Reveals Partial Overlap with First Episode Psychosis
post: Aim: Compare the acute effects of LSD with medication-naive first episode psychosis on resting-state functional connectivity using connectome-based classification. Methods: Connectome-based classifiers trained separately on LSD versus placebo and on first episode psychosis versus healthy controls, with the LSD classifier validated externally and cross-applied between datasets. Results: Cross-application revealed partial overlap between LSD and psychosis, particularly involving the dorsal attention and sensorimotor networks. Univariate analysis supported between-network dysconnectivity in these networks as a point of convergence. Conclusion: Neural correlates of first episode psychosis partly overlap with LSD-induced changes, suggesting a possible serotonergic contribution, and direct comparative studies are needed.

title: Psychedelic experience intensity during ketamine treatment and antidepressant outcomes.
post: Aim: Test whether subjective psychedelic intensity during ketamine treatment is associated with antidepressant outcomes beyond an adverse-event framing. Methods: Retrospective longitudinal cohort of 3,637 adults with moderate-to-severe depression receiving up to four sublingual ketamine doses over four weeks, with subjective effects measured by the five-item Mindbloom Psychedelic Intensity scale at midpoint. Results: Higher intensity scores at two weeks were associated with greater PHQ-9 reduction at four weeks, higher likelihood of clinically significant change, and greater membership of an improvement trajectory, independent of dose and covariates. Conclusion: Subjective intensity of the ketamine experience is robustly associated with antidepressant response, although the retrospective design limits causal inference.

title: Psilocybin induces delayed and dynamic changes in human sleep neurophysiology: Results from a randomized controlled trial of psilocybin assisted therapy in patients with comorbid major depressive and alcohol use disorder
post: Aim: Characterise the acute and post-acute temporal dynamics of sleep neurophysiology after psilocybin-assisted therapy in comorbid depression and alcohol use disorder. Methods: Randomised placebo-controlled trial with 40 participants (psilocybin n=22, placebo n=18), home sleep EEG for three nights before and seven nights after administration, analysed with nonlinear mixed-effects models. Results: Delayed, nonlinear changes emerged after psilocybin, with NREM slow-wave activity, sigma and REM beta peaking or troughing around 3–4 nights post-administration. Sleep efficiency and total sleep time increased over the first three post-treatment nights, while architecture changes were largely absent. Conclusion: Psilocybin-assisted therapy induces delayed, dynamic sleep EEG changes beyond the acute period, suggesting sleep EEG may be a sensitive measure of evolving neurophysiology.

title: Psychedelics and Sleep: Preclinical and Human Studies-A Systematic Review.
post: Background: Classic psychedelics, including LSD, psilocybin, and N,N-dimethyltryptamine (DMT)/ayahuasca, have shown promise as rapid-acting treatments for psychiatric disorders. Methods: A systematic review was conducted following PRISMA guidelines. Study validity was assessed using appropriate methodological tools. Results: Preclinical studies consistently demonstrated acute REM sleep suppression, delayed REM onset, increased wakefulness, and transient disruption of non-REM sleep. Human findings were more heterogeneous, although randomized trials reported prolonged REM latency after psilocybin and reduced REM duration after ayahuasca. Conclusion: Classic psychedelics produce acute but transient alterations in sleep physiology, particularly affecting REM sleep.

title: Modelling vortex interactions reveals distinct patterns of brain reconfiguration following psilocybin and escitalopram
post: Aim: Determine how psilocybin and escitalopram reshape brain dynamics in depression, and whether vortex-space modelling captures treatment effects better than signal-space modelling. Methods: Pre- and post-treatment resting-state fMRI from a double-blind randomised controlled trial of psilocybin versus escitalopram in depression, compared using signal-space and vortex-space whole-brain models. Results: Vortex-space modelling was more sensitive than signal-space modelling in most analyses. Psilocybin increased vortex-space effective connectivity and reduced modularity, whereas escitalopram showed no comparable change. Greater increases in brain turbulence were associated with symptom reduction in both treatments. Conclusion: The two treatments reorganise brain dynamics in markedly different ways yet share features linked to clinical improvement, and vortex-space modelling is a promising framework for depression.

title: Psilocybin desynchronizes the human brain
post: Aim: To determine how psilocybin reshapes large-scale human brain functional connectivity and whether these changes relate to the subjective experience and lasting effects. Methods: Longitudinal precision fMRI with roughly 18 scans per participant in healthy adults, before, during and for three weeks after 25 mg psilocybin or 40 mg methylphenidate, with a further psilocybin dose 6-12 months later. Results: Psilocybin produced over threefold greater acute connectivity change than methylphenidate, driven by cross-scale desynchronisation, strongest in the default mode network. Anterior hippocampus to default mode connectivity stayed reduced for weeks. Conclusion: Persistent hippocampal-default mode reduction may be a neuroanatomical correlate of the proplasticity and therapeutic effects of psychedelics. The sample is small and healthy-volunteer based.
why_you: Core to your interest in psychedelics as neuroplastogens and to the default-mode and hippocampal network changes you measure.

title: Psilocybin for treatment-resistant depression: fMRI-measured brain mechanisms
post: Aim: To characterise the brain mechanisms, measured with fMRI, of psilocybin-assisted treatment for treatment-resistant depression. Methods: Pre and post-treatment fMRI measuring cerebral blood flow and BOLD resting-state connectivity in 19 patients treated with psilocybin and psychological support, with 16 having quality scans. Results: All 19 patients showed reduced depressive symptoms at one week, and 47% responded at five weeks. Reduced amygdala blood flow correlated with symptom reduction, and default-mode connectivity increased post-treatment. Conclusion: Post-treatment brain changes differ from acute psychedelic effects yet relate to clinical outcomes. The authors propose a reset mechanism, with small sample size as a limitation.

title: Scale-rich network-based metamaterials.
post: Aim: To embed network heterogeneity into mechanical metamaterials and test whether multiscale variability yields properties unavailable to single-scale designs. Methods: Two-parameter scale-rich network models translated into physical materials, evaluated through simulations and experiments on elastic, nonlinear, dynamic and wave-control behaviour. Results: Scale-rich metamaterials showed highly tunable elastic anisotropy, delocalised nonlinear deformation with high energy absorption, enhanced energy dissipation under dynamic loading and programmable elastic-wave control. Conclusion: The framework provides a minimal, universal model for engineering multifunctional materials whose mechanics emerge from scale diversity, and opens new questions for network science.

title: Human land use drives microplastic abundance in terrestrial wildlife.
authors: Marcia de Almeida Monteiro Melo Ferraz
post: Aim: To determine how human land use and the animals' proximity to development shape microplastic burdens in terrestrial wildlife. Methods: In vivo microplastic measurements in blood and tissue of free-ranging lowland tapirs and giant anteaters across Brazil, paired with high-resolution GPS tracking and human footprint exposure data. Results: Microplastic burdens increased with human footprint exposure and proximity to development and waste management infrastructure. Microplastics were also detected in individuals in seemingly pristine habitats far from development. Conclusion: Direct exposure to modified landscapes is unlikely to be the sole driver of systemic burdens. Managing proximity to development and waste infrastructure may reduce wildlife microplastic exposure.
why_you: Loosely relevant: a neuroscientist may find the systemic, non-local exposure pattern an interesting parallel to how environmental factors reach the brain.

title: A Neandertal-derived genetic variant reduces occipital brain volume in present-day humans
venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
venue_clean: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
post: Aim: Whether a Neandertal-derived genetic variant influences occipital brain volume and schizophrenia risk in present-day humans. Methods: Genetic association analysis linking a Neandertal-inherited variant near DAAM1 to occipital lobe volume, gene expression, schizophrenia risk and cognitive measures. Results: Carriers had occipital volumes about 0.85 cm³ smaller per gene copy. Homozygous carriers showed almost 10% lower schizophrenia risk, with little or no association with cognition or schooling. Conclusion: The authors conclude the variant alters brain anatomy and lowers schizophrenia risk with little association with general cognitive ability.

post: Aim: To develop a non-invasive 7T EEG-fMRI framework for studying the generating mechanisms of alpha oscillations across cortical depth. Results: In 9 of 10 participants, EEG alpha power correlated negatively with visual cortex BOLD. Conclusion: The authors state the depth profiles are consistent with top-down feedback activity, but causality cannot be definitively demonstrated from these data.

title: Domain-level symptom improvement after ketamine and TMS-based stimulation in treatment-resistant depression: a post hoc pooled analysis.
post: Aim: Whether ketamine and TMS produce different short-term improvements across depression, anxiety, insomnia and somatic symptom domains. Methods: Post hoc pooled analysis of 159 active-treatment participants from three trials, ketamine infusion (n=89) or two-week TMS (n=70), with domain-level models adjusted for baseline scores, age and sex. Conclusion: The authors caution that cross-modality comparisons are exploratory and do not establish equivalence or guide treatment choice.

title: Default Mode Network Modulation by Psychedelics: A Systematic Review
post: Background: Psychedelics are a unique class of drug that commonly produce vivid hallucinations as well as profound psychological and mystical experiences. Methods: To date, several studies have investigated how psychedelics modulate this network, but no comprehensive review, to our knowledge, has critically evaluated how major classical psychedelic agents-lysergic acid diethylamide, psilocybin, and ayahuasca-modulate the DMN. Results: Across psychedelics there is consistent acute disruption in resting state connectivity within the DMN and increased functional connectivity between canonical resting-state networks. Various models have been proposed to explain the cognitive mechanisms of psychedelics, and in one model DMN modulation is a central axiom. Conclusion: This article aims to provide the field with a comprehensive overview that can propel future research in such a way as to elucidate the neurocognitive mechanisms of psychedelics.

post: Aim: This study investigated whether repeated prefrontal tDCS improves behavioral outcomes and reorganizes resting-state electroencephalographic (EEG) microstate dynamics in young adults with PSU. Methods: Eighty participants meeting validated criteria for PSU were randomly assigned to receive active (n = 40) or sham (n = 40) tDCS. Results: Compared with sham stimulation, active tDCS significantly reduced objectively measured smartphone use, craving intensity, and functional impairment while improving behavioral regulation. During eyes-closed recording, microstate C occurrence decreased whereas microstate D occurrence increased significantly. Conclusion: These findings provide preliminary evidence that repeated prefrontal tDCS is associated with concurrent behavioral changes and alterations in resting-state EEG microstate dynamics in young adults with PSU.

title: Cortical-fluidic dimensional mapping isolates GRIN2A-driven dysconnectivity and pharmacological network degradation in schizophrenia.
post: Background: Standard connectivity models fail to capture the transient spatial kinematics underlying schizophrenia pathophysiology. Methods: The algorithm processed over 7000 memory testing sessions from 364 healthy participants. The validation phase evaluated a pre-existing clinical repository comprising 300 de-identified psychiatric records. Results: Cuneus dysconnectivity links strictly to global symptom severity. The methodology establishes an objective biomarker. Conclusion: The system links molecular glutamatergic vulnerabilities to macroscopic neural degradation in treatment-resistant psychiatric conditions.

title: Dynamic epigenetic changes during antidepressant pharmacotherapy in major depressive disorder.
post: Background: Although antidepressants remain the main pharmacological treatment for major depressive disorder (MDD), therapeutic response varies, highlighting the need for molecular markers that predict treatment response, as well as insights into the biological … Methods: To date, no longitudinal EWAS has examined methylation trajectories across multiple time points during antidepressant treatment in MDD. Results: Baseline methylation levels were associated with depressive symptom severity at day 28 and day 56 through two and six DMRs, respectively (e.g., TNRC6C, CAT), whereas no single DMP reached significance. title: Gender differences in depressive-like behavior in Parkinson's disease.
post: Background: Although sex differences have been described in PD progression, the mechanisms underlying gender-specific susceptibility to depressive symptoms remain poorly understood. Methods: This study investigated sex-dependent differences in depressive-like behaviors and their underlying molecular mechanisms in an in vivo model of 1-methyl-4-phenyl-1,2,3,6-tetrahydropyridine (MPTP)-induced dopaminergic degeneration, using adult male and female CD1 mice. Results: Our results demonstrated that MPTP administration induced nigrostriatal degeneration and α-synuclein accumulation in both sexes, with more pronounced alterations in males. Conclusion: Overall, our results highlight the importance of considering sex as a biological variable in PD research and support the development of personalized therapeutic strategies targeting non-motor symptoms.

title: Cannabidiol prevents fear extinction deficits caused by single prolonged stress in rats: possible involvement of serotoninergic, cannabinoid, and nitric mechanisms.
post: Background: Post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) involves impaired extinction learning, autonomic and neuroendocrine dysregulation, and first-line selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) show limited efficacy. Methods: We investigated effects and mechanisms of cannabidiol (CBD) on fear deficits induced by the single prolonged stress (SPS) model in male Wistar rats. Results: Repeated CBD (5 and 10 mg/kg, 7 days) prevented extinction memory impairments, and these effects were attenuated by the 5-HT1A antagonist WAY-100635 and the CB1 antagonist AM281. Conclusion: These findings indicate that CBD prevents SPS-induced extinction deficits through 5-HT1A- and CB1-dependent mechanisms, identify nNOS as a candidate downstream substrate, and support CBD as a multi-target candidate for PTSD treatment.

title: Endogenous suspension of phenomenal consciousness during extended cessation: Regional homogeneity analysis of multi-participant 7T fMRI of an advanced meditative endpoint.
post: Background: Extended cessation (EC) is a rare advanced meditative state characterized by the voluntary absence of reportable phenomenal experience, followed by reproducible aftereffects including immense mental clarity, equanimity, and peace. Methods: In a small-N case study (N = 3) using ultra-high-resolution 7T functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) with dense within-subject sampling, we quantified whole-brain activity and related it to chemoarchitecture and cognitive maps. Results: EC is marked by increased activity in unimodal sensory cortices and viscerosensory brainstem nuclei, and down-regulation in transmodal regions, subcortex and brainstem. Multivariate coupling to normative neurotransmitter maps revealed that EC-related connectivity changes covaried with histaminergic H 3 receptors topology. Conclusion: These findings constrain prevailing theories of consciousness by demonstrating that loss of experience need not entail global neural suppression, and supports accounts emphasizing selective precision modulation and hierarchical decoupling.

title: Comprehensive benchmarking of EEG biomarkers for Parkinson's disease: robustness, reliability, and clinical discriminability across multiple datasets.
post: Background: Electroencephalography (EEG) provides a high-temporal-resolution, noninvasive window into some of the abnormalities underlying Parkinson's disease (PD), yet reported electrophysiological biomarkers vary widely across studies due to differences in preprocessing, feature extraction … Methods: Here we provide the first comprehensive, multi-dataset benchmarking of 16 EEG-derived biomarkers, including phase-amplitude coupling, beta burst metrics, aperiodic components, complexity measures, and beta waveform features, to evaluate their robustness, reliability, and clinical discriminability. Results: In contrast, oscillatory biomarkers, including beta-gamma phase-amplitude coupling, burst-derived metrics, and waveform-asymmetry features, showed substantial variability across methodological choices and lower within-session consistency. Conclusion: Together, these findings identify several biomarkers with comparatively strong methodological robustness for further biological and clinical validation and highlight methodological factors that contribute to inconsistencies in the PD literature.

title: Mechanism-guided generative chemistry yields distinct agonist-like and antagonist-like ligand populations for the serotonin 5-HT2A receptor
post: Background: Designing serotonin 5-HT2A receptor ligands with a specified functional direction is difficult because binding affinity, assay-derived mechanism labels, molecular properties and receptor conformation are only partially coupled. Methods: We developed a mechanism-guided generative chemistry workflow integrating curated ChEMBL data, scaffold-aware supervised learning, a recurrent SMILES prior, reinforcement learning, medicinal-chemistry prioritization, receptor-context docking, MM-GBSA rescoring and property-adjusted contact analysis. Results: Antagonist-like candidates showed higher predicted affinity and mechanism-label confidence, whereas agonist-like candidates showed higher QED, greater internal diversity and lower training-set similarity. Conclusion: The study identifies distinct model-defined chemical regimes and links campaign-level property drift to receptor-contact topology; generated compounds remain computational hypotheses requiring experimental validation.

title: From Evidence to Practice: A Systematic Review of Implementation of Psychedelic-Assisted Psychotherapy.
post: Aim: The specific objectives of this systematic review were to: (1) identify extant literature on implementation of PAP, and (2) synthesize and present findings to understand current implementation knowledge and inform future directions. Methods: This systematic review followed the procedures outlined in Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses 2020. Results: A total of 2,406 articles were identified, and 2,074 of these were screened by title and abstract after the initial elimination of duplicates and sources that were not peer-reviewed research articles (e.g., gray literature). Forty-seven were retrieved for full text review, and 20 studies were included in the review. Conclusion: There is a noticeable gap in implementation-focused research on best practices for translating PAP from academic settings into accessible clinical programs.

title: The molecular and neurochemical basis of altered intrinsic neural timescales in major depressive disorder: a multimodal imaging-transcriptomic investigation of esketamine and sertraline treatment.
post: Background: Major depressive disorder (MDD) is characterized by dysfunction in higher-order cortical regions involved in emotional and cognitive processes; however, its neurobiological basis remains unclear.
